title: Dhruva, the boy who became the pole star
hook: a five-year-old's prayer holds so steady that Vishnu sets him in the sky, and it's why a Hindu couple is shown the pole star

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dattatreya's wasp, and the rule under the powers. You become what you dwell on.
screen: `THE WASP — YOU BECOME WHAT YOU DWELL ON.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata tells of a boy named Dhruva. He's five. He climbs onto his father the king's lap, and his stepmother pulls him off: if you wanted that lap, she says, you should have been born to me. He runs to his mother, crying. She doesn't fight back. She tells him only the Lord can give him a place no one can take. So the five-year-old walks into the forest to find the Lord.
screen: `A BOY PULLED OFF A LAP.` → `INTO THE FOREST.` → `TO FIND THE LORD.`

segments.voice: On the way, the sage Narada tests him: you're a child, go home. Dhruva won't. So Narada gives him a mantra, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, and a way to sit. Dhruva prays by the Yamuna for months, eating less and less, until he stands on one foot, and the story says the whole world feels his weight. Vishnu comes. And here's the turn: Dhruva finds he no longer wants what he came for. He went looking for a lap and found the Lord. Vishnu gives him a place anyway, the star that never moves, the one point the whole night sky turns around. Dhruva means fixed, steady. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, steadiness is itself devotion, and God answers a prayer that doesn't move, even a child's. You can see it at a Hindu wedding. In many weddings, the priest shows the couple the pole star, Dhruva, as a picture of a marriage that holds. Now Patanjali points samyama at the sky. Sutra 3.26, on the sun: knowledge of the worlds. 3.27, on the moon: how the stars are arranged. 3.28, on the pole star: how they move. Fix on the one point that doesn't move, and you can read the motion of everything else. Then 3.29 comes down to the body's own center, the navel. It's why so many Hindus keep one prayer every single day, the way Dhruva kept his mantra. When a week won't stop moving, that prayer is the point that doesn't.
screen: `NARADA'S MANTRA.` · `A PRAYER THAT DOESN'T MOVE.` · `VISHNU: THE FIXED STAR.` · `THE WEDDING: SHOWN THE POLE STAR.` · `3.28: REST ON WHAT'S STILL.` · then, large: `DEVOTION THAT DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: Let your attention rest on one point. If you pray, make it the name Narada gave Dhruva, om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, said slowly. If you don't, make it the navel, rising and falling with the breath. Thoughts will move around it like the night sky turning. You don't have to stop them. Stay with the one point, and watch the rest move.
Dhruva: fixed, steady. The pole star, and the boy who became it, with a prayer that didn't move.
Your line: dhruva, devotion that doesn't move. A child's steady prayer, set in the sky. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Dhruva's story is commonly told to Hindu children, Narada's twelve-syllable mantra to Vishnu is widely chanted, and in many Hindu weddings the couple is shown the pole star as a sign of a steady marriage; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 3.26–3.29 as samyama moving from the sky to the body's center.

fork.reveal: Dhruva came for his father's lap and found the Lord. in Hinduism steady devotion is itself the gift, and God answers it, even from a five-year-old.

original.note: Sanskrit dhruva: fixed, steady; the pole star, and the name of the boy in the Puranas who became it.

samyama.meaning: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object
